attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own post. He cites reporting nearby, but this conclusion is his.

semantics.note: 'Such returns' refers to the profit-based returns (and cap) discussed just before. The normalised wording keeps 'at best theoretical' and both stated reasons. It is an as-of observation, partly evaluative.

contract.note: The contract reads 'returns' as profit distributions, not resale gains, and 'theoretical' as not yet realised. Both fit the context ('500% of nothing'). The September 2024 window is a reasonable as-of reading.

evidence.note: Sherwood (Sept 10, 2024) explains that PPUs pay only from future profits and says OpenAI is far from profitable. It is not a distribution record, and it notes that PPUs can be resold.
OpenAI's own 2019 description of the capped-profit structure. It is a company disclosure about structure, not evidence of whether distributions happened in 2024.

reviews.rationale: Neither item shows whether any profit distributions were paid to investors as of September 2024. The contract asks for distribution records or reporting on realised profit returns. The context about unprofitability fits the claim but does not settle it, so the claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own prediction in his own post.

semantics.note: Firm 'will', conditional on failing to show a significant revenue increase. The antecedent and the 'next quarter' horizon are kept. '$150bn' describes the investment, not a threshold, and the contract treats it that way.

contract.note: Reading 'face the wheel' as an adverse earnings reaction and 'next quarter' as the October 2024 earnings cycle is ordinary and fair. Applying the condition to each company is reasonable. The speaker gave no threshold for 'significant', so the antecedent depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: Microsoft's own disclosure: AI contributed about 12 points of Azure growth, similar to the prior quarter. This leaves the antecedent unclear for Microsoft.
Google reports 35% cloud revenue growth, which is total cloud revenue, not AI revenue. It does not settle the antecedent.

Amazon earnings call (third-party transcript): AWS AI is described as a multibillion-dollar run rate growing at triple digits. This is an annualised company claim and points against the antecedent for Amazon.
Reuters, Oct 31, 2024: Microsoft down 5.6% intraday amid concern about AI costs. Shows the reaction but not that the revenue condition was met.
Reuters, Nov 1, 2024: Amazon up 7% intraday after earnings. Not contradiction, because Amazon's antecedent is not established.
Reuters, Oct 30, 2024: Alphabet up 2.8% after earnings. Not contradiction without the antecedent.

reviews.rationale: The horizon has passed, but the packet does not show that any of the three companies failed to show significant AI revenue growth. Microsoft and Amazon reported material AI growth on their own measures. Because the antecedent is not established, the forecast cannot be scored: Microsoft's drop does not confirm it, and the gains at Amazon and Alphabet do not refute it.

attribution.note: Zitron's own statement. The supporting figures he gives come from The Information, but the claim itself is his.

semantics.note: The normalised proposition matches the statement: an unqualified present-tense claim of deep unprofitability.

contract.note: Reading it as an aggregate operating loss after attributable costs, using H1 2024, is an ordinary reading. How training and research costs are allocated could decide the result, and the contract says so.

evidence.note: FutureSearch estimates an API gross margin of about 75% in June 2024. It covers only the API, gross margin only, and is self-described as unverified. It does not measure aggregate operating profit, so it cannot contradict the claim.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no matched H1 2024 product revenue and attributable operating costs. The only item is an API gross-margin estimate, which neither establishes nor refutes an aggregate operating loss. The claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own statement in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps both parts: pressure for training data, and 'almost every' LLM having ingested copyrighted material. The 'to the point that' link is noted in the contract and not tested.

contract.note: Reading 'almost every' as an overwhelming majority without a numeric cutoff, counting licensed works as copyrighted, and reading 'desperate' as material supply pressure are fair, ordinary readings.

evidence.note: Peer-style study showing OpenAI models (and BERT) memorised in-copyright books. Consistent with the claim, but it covers too few model families to establish prevalence across LLMs.
July 2024 audit finding rapidly rising restrictions on web training data. Supports the data-pressure part only.
Epoch (June 2024) projects that available text will be exhausted in 2026-2032. Rules out a literal-exhaustion reading of 'desperate' but fits current pressure.

reviews.rationale: The data-pressure part has some support (e2). The main assertion, that almost every LLM ingested copyrighted material, has no representative census in the packet, only examples from a few model families. Nothing contradicts either part, but the prevalence part is not settled, so the claim as a whole is unresolved.
